lesson.title: The Movement That Split a Nation
lesson.summary: As the Vietnam War dragged on and the Tet Offensive exposed the gap between official optimism and battlefield reality, an increasingly broad coalition of students, clergy, veterans, and ordinary citizens organized a sustained movement to end US involvement in the war.
lesson.body:
Organized opposition to the Vietnam War began well before Tet, rooted mostly on college campuses. Groups like Students for a Democratic Society and gatherings known as teach-ins, informal campus events where faculty and students debated the war outside the normal classroom setting, starting at the University of Michigan in March 1965, gave early opposition a foothold. Through the mid 1960s, though, war critics remained a minority voice, often dismissed as fringe or unpatriotic.

The Tet Offensive changed that. Once the credibility of official claims about the war's progress broke down, opposition spread well beyond students to clergy, civil rights leaders, journalists, and even members of Congress and the foreign policy establishment. Large demonstrations followed, including a march on the Pentagon in October 1967 and, after Tet, chaotic and violently policed protests outside the Democratic National Convention in Chicago in August 1968. In October 1969, the Moratorium to End the War in Vietnam brought out millions of participants nationwide in one of the largest coordinated protests in American history, involving far more than students alone.

The military draft gave the movement much of its urgency and exposed deep inequities in the war's burden, since deferments for college enrollment and other exemptions meant that working class and poor Americans, including a disproportionate share of Black Americans, were more likely to be drafted and sent to fight. A lottery system introduced in December 1969 was meant to make the draft fairer, but it did not resolve the underlying anger over who was being asked to fight and die. Veterans themselves became a powerful voice against the war through organizations such as Vietnam Veterans Against the War.

Not all Americans supported the movement. President Nixon, who took office in January 1969, appealed directly in a November 1969 address to what he called the silent majority of Americans who, he argued, quietly supported the war effort even as protests dominated headlines. The country grew visibly split between those demanding an immediate end to the war and those who saw the protests themselves as a threat to social order, a division that would explode into tragedy the following spring when Nixon expanded the war into Cambodia.
